\begin{abstract}
Latent world models plan by scoring imagined rollouts against a goal
embedding. LeWorldModel (LeWM) trains on a short window of four images
and uses the short-horizon Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) with a Euclidean
terminal cost. When the goal lies beyond one planning horizon, this
cost compares a near-term predicted latent with a still-distant goal
embedding. Existing approaches modify the predictor, the planning
hierarchy, or the distance metric. We instead treat terminal scoring as
a temporal correspondence problem: the two arguments of the Euclidean
cost should refer to the same remaining time. Horizon-Aligned Scoring
(HAS) trains an action-free forward imaginer $F$ on detached latents
and replaces the LeWM cost with
$C_F=\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\|^2$. $F$ maps the short-plan endpoint toward the
goal horizon before the distance is evaluated. Across $10$ evaluation
seeds on PushT and TwoRoom, HAS and LeWM coincide at offset $25$
($k{=}0$). Beyond one horizon, HAS raises PushT success from $42.8\%$
to $67.8\%$ at offset $50$ and TwoRoom success from $16.4\%$ to
$70.4\%$ at offset $100$.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Latent world models enable goal-conditioned control by scoring imagined
rollouts in representation
space~\citep{hafner2019planet,hafner2020dreamer,hansen2022tdmpc}.
LeWorldModel (LeWM)~\citep{lewm2026} implements this approach with an
action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture
(JEPA)~\citep{lecun2022jepa}: an encoder $E$ produces latent
representations, a predictor $P$ rolls them forward under candidate
actions, and the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)~\citep{rubinstein1999cem}
selects an action sequence using terminal Euclidean distance to a goal
embedding $\zg$.

This terminal cost becomes problematic when the goal lies beyond one
planning horizon. LeWM performs well when the goal is reachable within
a short plan, but at longer offsets CEM must rank short plans by
comparing a near-term predicted latent with a still-distant $\zg$.
Recent work addresses long-horizon planning by lengthening the
action-conditioned
predictor~\citep{du2026vlwm}, planning at several resolutions or toward
predicted
subgoals~\citep{zhang2026hwm,masip2026ffjepa,cheng2026sage}, or
replacing Euclidean MSE with a learned metric~\citep{li2026trm}. These
approaches modify the predictive horizon, planning hierarchy, or
scoring function. We instead study the temporal semantics of terminal
scoring: how should a planner compare a near-term predicted endpoint
with a goal representation from a later stage of the trajectory?

We introduce Horizon-Aligned Scoring (HAS). A small action-free
imaginer $F$ learns a forward temporal map in latent space. At planning
time, $F$ is applied $k$ times to the predicted endpoint so that
$\Fk(\Pend)$ and $\zg$ refer to a shared remaining horizon. CEM then
ranks candidate plans by Euclidean distance between this pair. HAS does
not claim that $F$ reconstructs future encoder states. It only changes
the temporal arguments of the terminal cost used to order short plans.

This paper makes three contributions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Problem formulation.} We identify temporal mismatch
between the predicted endpoint and the goal embedding as a failure
mode of Euclidean terminal costs in short-horizon latent planning.
\item \textbf{Horizon-aligned scoring.} We introduce HAS, which uses an
action-free forward imaginer to form the terminal cost
$C_F=\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\|^2$.
\item \textbf{Empirical evaluation.} Over $10$ evaluation seeds on
PushT and TwoRoom, HAS raises success once the goal leaves one
planning horizon, including a TwoRoom gain from $16.4\%$ to $70.4\%$
at offset $100$.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

Visual MPC and latent imagination score candidate actions by rolling a
learned model~\citep{hafner2019planet,hafner2020dreamer}. TD-MPC,
DINO-WM, and LeWM use CEM (or MPPI) with a terminal latent
distance~\citep{hansen2022tdmpc,zhou2025dinowm,lewm2026}. The default
metric is Euclidean MSE between the predicted endpoint and $\zg$.

Several recent papers attack long-offset failure by changing a
different piece of that stack. VLWM trains an action-conditioned
predictor on variable-length action chunks so $P$ can jump $k$ steps
in one
query~\citep{du2026vlwm}. HWM plans at several temporal resolutions
and uses coarse predictions as subgoals for short-horizon
MPC~\citep{zhang2026hwm}. FF-JEPA adds an action-free forward model
that proposes the next subgoal, then runs CEM to that
subgoal~\citep{masip2026ffjepa}. SAGE keeps frozen LeWM and CEM, but
conditions the \emph{proposal} distribution on a predicted
subgoal~\citep{cheng2026sage}. On the cost side, temporal
straightening regularizes latent trajectories so Euclidean distance
better tracks geodesic progress~\citep{wang2026straightening}, and
trajectory reachability metrics (TRM) replace or mix terminal MSE with
a pairwise head trained on horizon-matched temporal
separations~\citep{li2026trm}.

Prior work can therefore lengthen $P$, introduce hierarchical or
subgoal-conditioned search, or learn a new distance metric. HAS
instead formulates terminal scoring as a temporal correspondence
problem: before evaluating distance, $F$ advances $\Pend$ so that the
compared representations refer to a shared horizon. The closest
cost-side method is TRM: both identify candidate ranking as a source of
long-horizon failure, but TRM learns a scalar reachability metric,
whereas HAS constructs a temporally matched representation for
latent-space scoring.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{LeWM}
\label{sec:lewm}

We follow LeWM's training path. A window of four encoded
observations $z_{0:3}=E(o_{0:3})$ and the corresponding actions is fed
to $P$. Prediction targets are the encoder latents. The loss is
next-embedding MSE plus SIGReg,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LeWM}}
=\underbrace{\|P(z,a)-z_{\mathrm{next}}\|^2}_{\mathrm{pred}}
+0.09\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SIGReg}}(z).
\end{equation}
At evaluation, CEM always plans $\planlen$ environment steps
(horizon $5$, receding horizon $5$, action block $5$). The LeWM cost is
$\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$, where $\Pend$ is the predicted embedding after those
$25$ steps.

\subsection{Horizon-aligned scoring}
\label{sec:imaginers}

The LeWM cost compares $\Pend$ at time $t{+}25$ to a goal that may be
many action-blocks further. HAS inserts a residual MLP $F$ that reads
stop-gradient copies of $P$'s output $p$. Imaginer losses train only
$F$. With a four-step window, $p_1,p_2,p_3$ align with $z_1,z_2,z_3$.

$F$ maps a predicted latent toward a later encoder latent,
\begin{equation}
F(p_1)\to z_2,\qquad F(p_2)\to z_3,\qquad F(F(p_1))\to z_3,
\end{equation}
with equal weight on the one-step and two-step terms. The HAS planning
cost is
\begin{equation}
C_F=\bigl\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\bigr\|^2.
\end{equation}
This cost is used only to rank CEM samples. We do not treat
$\Fk(\Pend)$ as a calibrated forecast of a future encoder state.

For goal offset $o$ and elapsed time $t$, the imagination depth is
\begin{equation}
k=\max\bigl((o-t-\planlen)/5,\,0\bigr).
\end{equation}
The division by $5$ matches the action block. When $k{=}0$, $F$ is
skipped and $C_F=\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$. Offset $25$ at the first replan
therefore has $k{=}0$, so HAS and LeWM share the same cost.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:exp}

We compare LeWM and HAS on one frozen checkpoint per task (epoch $10$).
Each evaluation seed draws $n{=}50$ episodes. We report mean $\pm$
standard deviation over seeds $42$--$51$. The interaction budget is
twice the goal offset ($50$, $100$, $150$, $200$ steps at offsets
$25$, $50$, $75$, $100$). CEM uses horizon $5$ at every offset
($25$ environment steps). Success is the environment criterion on
PushT~\citep{florence2022ibc} and TwoRoom.

At offset $25$, $k{=}0$, so HAS reduces to the LeWM cost. The two
methods therefore coincide there by construction
(Table~\ref{tab:main}, Figure~\ref{fig:multiseed}). The comparison
begins at offsets $50$--$100$, where the goal lies beyond one short
plan.

\subsection{PushT}
\label{sec:pusht}

On PushT, HAS improves mid-range ranking after the goal leaves one
horizon: mean success rises from $42.8\%$ to $67.8\%$ at offset $50$
($+25.0$ points) and from $21.6\%$ to $40.4\%$ at offset $75$
($+18.8$ points). The gain remains positive at offset $100$
($13.2\%\to 23.4\%$), but absolute success stays low. HAS therefore
helps when the terminal pair is only moderately misaligned; it does
not turn a long PushT offset into a reliable short-horizon plan.

\subsection{TwoRoom}
\label{sec:tworoom}

TwoRoom isolates the same mismatch more cleanly. LeWM is already
strong at offset $25$ ($84.4\%$) and then falls to $42.4/25.8/16.4$
as the offset increases. HAS holds $80.4/82.0/70.4$ at those longer
offsets, a mean gain of $+38.0$, $+56.2$, and $+54.0$ points. Every
evaluation seed is positive beyond offset $25$. The TwoRoom gain does
not require $F$ to match encoder scale: after SIGReg warmup, $F$
outputs remain near $5.6$ against targets near $13.7$. CEM only has
to order candidates.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}

These results use one training seed and one checkpoint per task. The
controlled baseline is LeWM under the same $25$-step CEM; we do not
yet compare against a longer-horizon LeWM planner, or against VLWM,
HWM, SAGE, or TRM. PushT at offset $100$ remains $23.4\%$ under HAS.
Cube is not included in this draft.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:concl}

HAS treats the Euclidean terminal cost of short-horizon latent
planning as a temporal correspondence problem. An action-free forward
imaginer maps the predicted endpoint toward the goal horizon before
distance is evaluated. Over $10$ evaluation seeds, this scoring change
raises PushT mid-range success by $19$--$25$ points and TwoRoom
success at offset $100$ from $16.4\%$ to $70.4\%$. The working object
is the temporal pair supplied to CEM, not a longer action-conditioned
predictor.

involve human subjects, personal data, or deployed decision systems.
The usual dual-use concerns of motor-control research apply only at a
remove: the methods are evaluated in standard simulation benchmarks.

\subsection*{Reproducibility statement}

Section~\ref{sec:exp} states the evaluation protocol: $10$ evaluation
seeds ($42$--$51$), $n{=}50$ episodes per seed, interaction budget
$2\times$ the goal offset, epoch-10 checkpoints, and CEM horizon $5$
at every offset. Training losses and the imagination depth $k$ are
given in Section~\ref{sec:method}. Configurations and scripts used to
produce Table~\ref{tab:main} will be included with the code release.

\appendix
\section{Protocol details}
\label{app:protocol}

CEM uses \texttt{horizon=5}, \texttt{receding=5}, and
\texttt{action\_block=5}, so one plan is $\planlen$ environment steps.
The evaluation budget is $2\times$ the goal offset. Imagination depth
is $k=\max((o-t-25)/5,\,0)$. The LeWM cost is $\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$; HAS
uses $\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\|^2$. When $k{=}0$, $F$ is skipped.

Each seed in $\{42,\ldots,51\}$ draws $50$ starts independently. The
numbers in Table~\ref{tab:main} are mean and standard deviation of
those per-seed success rates.
